title: State v. Roberts
description: Whether the state's failure to appoint counsel for an eligible criminal defendant for an extended period violates the right to counsel under Article I, section 11 of the Oregon Constitution, and if so, whether dismissal of the criminal case without prejudice is an appropriate remedy.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the failure to appoint counsel does not violate the right to counsel unless it causes 'incurable prejudice' to the defendant, and dismissal is only required in such instances.
defendant_argument: The relator (defendant) argued that the state's complete and indefinite denial of counsel for months, while criminal charges remained pending and he was subject to liberty restraints, violated his right to counsel, and dismissal without prejudice after a certain period (e.g., 30 days) was the only constitutionally adequate remedy.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the alternative writ of mandamus as moot because the trial court had already dismissed the criminal case. However, the Supreme Court exercised its discretion to adjudicate the underlying constitutional questions, concluding that the state violated the relator's right to counsel and that dismissal without prejudice is required when counsel is not provided for more than 60 consecutive days in a misdemeanor case or 90 consecutive days in a felony case.

title: State v. Hemion
description: Whether the Washington County Circuit Court's order requiring Metropolitan Public Defender, Inc. (MPD) to disclose records regarding cases handled for its indigent clients was valid, with MPD arguing the legal bases were insufficient and the State of Oregon agreeing.
plaintiff_argument: Metropolitan Public Defender, Inc. (MPD) argued that the trial court's order, based on Article I, section 10, of the Oregon Constitution and the Public Records Law, was legally unsupported and erroneous.
defendant_argument: The State of Oregon (Adverse Party) agreed with MPD's argument that the trial court's legal bases for the order were erroneous and did not support the disclosure requirement.
decision_outcome: The court issued a peremptory writ of mandamus, directing the Washington County Circuit Court to vacate its order requiring Metropolitan Public Defender, Inc. to disclose records.

title: Scott-Schwalbach v. Rosenblum
description: Whether the Attorney General's certified ballot title for Initiative Petition 5 (2024) adequately describes the proposed measure's subject matter and major effects, specifically regarding parental school choice, the elimination of school district discretion, and the fiscal impact on school funding.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner argued that the ballot title was insufficient because it failed to adequately describe the elimination of school district discretion in admitting nonresident students and the non-speculative fiscal impact of funding following the student.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General argued that the ballot title accurately described the core legal effect of creating a new parental right and that the fiscal impact was not a direct effect or was speculative, thus not requiring inclusion.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the caption, the "yes" result statement, and the summary of the certified ballot title for Initiative Petition 5 all require modification.

title: Arnold v. Kotek
description: Whether Ballot Measure 114, which requires a permit to purchase a firearm, completion of a background check at the point-of-transfer, and limits lawful firearm magazine capacity to 10 or fewer rounds, is facially constitutional under Article I, section 27, of the Oregon Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing it unduly burdens the right to bear arms for self-defense and defendants arguing it is a reasonable regulation to promote public safety.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Measure 114 was facially unconstitutional, asserting that the permit-to-purchase program created undue burdens and delays, and that the large-capacity magazine ban effectively banned most firearms and did not enhance public safety.
defendant_argument: The defendants (the State) argued that Measure 114 is facially constitutional under Article I, section 27, as it represents a reasonable legislative response to identifiable public safety threats and does not unduly frustrate the right to armed self-defense.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals reversed the circuit court's judgment, holding that all of Ballot Measure 114 is facially valid under Article I, section 27, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

title: State v. Gonzalez
description: Whether a 90-month mandatory minimum sentence for defendant's convictions for first-degree arson would violate the proportionality clause of Article I, section 16, of the Oregon Constitution, which requires all penalties to be proportioned to the offense.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (State of Oregon) argued that the mandatory minimum sentence was not unconstitutionally disproportionate and that the trial court erred in relying on the defendant's personal characteristics and circumstances in its proportionality analysis.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Vanessa Amada Gonzalez) argued that the mandatory minimum sentence was unconstitutionally disproportionate as applied to her, contending that her mental illness should be considered a mitigating factor in the proportionality analysis, similar to intellectual disability.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that the 90-month mandatory minimum sentence for first-degree arson was not unconstitutionally disproportionate as applied to the defendant, and that the trial court erred in considering her mental health attributes in its proportionality analysis.

title: State v. Dodge
description: Whether the Court of Appeals erred in ruling that the defendant failed to preserve his argument that retrying him on previously convicted counts, after reversal, would violate double jeopardy due to the original indictment's lack of specificity.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the defendant's trial and appellate arguments were different, meaning he abandoned his trial argument and failed to preserve his appellate argument, and that retrial was permissible as a "continuing prosecution."
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that he consistently raised the same double jeopardy issue, contending that retrial on the remanded counts would violate his constitutional rights because the lack of specificity in the indictment and first trial created a risk of conviction for incidents he had already been acquitted of.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that the defendant had adequately preserved his double jeopardy argument, and remanded the case to the Court of Appeals for further proceedings on the merits of that argument.

title: Huskey v. Oregon Department of Corrections
description: Whether a plaintiff alleging economic damages in the form of future lost employment income must plead an "enforceable right" to that future employment to survive a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that he had properly pleaded economic damages for lost future wages and employment opportunities, and that Article I, section 41(3) of the Oregon Constitution did not require dismissal of his breach of contract claim, as he did in fact work and pleaded loss of income.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the plaintiff failed to allege facts showing economic damages because Article I, section 41(3) of the Oregon Constitution states that inmates have no legally enforceable right to a job or compensation for work, thus precluding a claim for lost income.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower courts' dismissal of the plaintiff's complaint, holding that a plaintiff does not need to plead an "enforceable right" to future employment to claim economic damages, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Autele
description: Whether a trial court can deny a criminal defendant's request to be represented by retained counsel of their choice without an adequate record demonstrating that the denial was a permissible exercise of discretion due to ethical conflicts or potential trial disruption.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the defendant failed to make an adequate record for appellate review, and alternatively, the trial court properly denied representation due to a "significant" ethical conflict.
defendant_argument: The defendant contended that the trial court erred by interfering with his choice of retained counsel because there was no evidence of an existing conflict of interest that would have delayed or disrupted the trial, and the record was inadequate.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals' decision is reversed, the judgment of the circuit court is reversed, and the case is remanded to the circuit court for a new trial.

title: Brown v. Kotek
description: Whether the Governor had the authority to revoke a conditional commutation after the plaintiff had already completed her sentence and post-prison supervision.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor lacked authority to revoke the conditional commutation because the plaintiff had finished serving all her sentences, and the waiver of rights in the acceptance agreement was invalid or unenforceable.
defendant_argument: The Governor had the authority to revoke the conditional commutation even after the plaintiff's sentence had expired, and the plaintiff had waived her right to challenge the revocation through the acceptance agreement.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Governor Kotek lacked the authority to revoke the plaintiff's conditional commutation because the plaintiff had already completed her sentence, and therefore, her present imprisonment was unlawful. The court ordered her immediate discharge from custody.

title: Thompson v. Fhuere
description: Whether the post-conviction court erred by modifying the petitioner's death sentence to life without the possibility of parole instead of remanding for resentencing, given the Governor's commutation and the procedural status of other claims.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that his death sentence and the penalty-phase questions were unconstitutional, requiring a remand for resentencing, and that the Governor's commutation did not preclude this relief.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Governor's commutation rendered the issue moot, and the post-conviction court correctly modified the sentence to life without parole, with the penalty-phase claims being procedurally barred.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the post-conviction court's judgment, upholding the modification of the death sentence to life without parole and ruling that the penalty-phase claims were procedurally barred.

title: Knopp v. Griffin-Valade
description: Whether the disqualification for legislators with 10 or more unexcused absences applies to the immediate next term of office or the term after that.
plaintiff_argument: The disqualification for legislators with 10 or more unexcused absences should apply one term later, meaning they serve the next term but are disqualified from the term after that.
defendant_argument: The disqualification for legislators with 10 or more unexcused absences should apply to the immediate next term of office following the term in which the absences occurred.
decision_outcome: The court upheld the Secretary of State's Temporary Rules ELECT 12-2023 and ELECT 16-2023, ruling that the disqualification applies to the immediate next term of office.

title: State v. Wilcox
description: Whether the warrantless seizure of a defendant's backpack during a non-criminal custody event for public intoxication was lawful under Article I, section 9, of the Oregon Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Court of Appeals erred by finding the seizure unlawful, contending the backpack was not seized, or if it was, it was a lawful administrative seizure, or a necessary byproduct of lawful custody.
defendant_argument: Wilcox argued that the Court of Appeals' decision that the warrantless seizure of his backpack was unlawful was correct and violated his rights against unreasonable search and seizure.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' decision and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, clarifying that the seizure should be analyzed under an administrative framework, not a criminal one.

title: State v. Reed
description: Whether police officers were required to advise the defendant of her Miranda rights before interrogating her in compelling circumstances, as mandated by Article I, section 12, of the Oregon Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the interrogation did not occur in compelling circumstances, therefore Miranda warnings were not required, and the evidence obtained should not be suppressed.
defendant_argument: Reed argued that the interrogation occurred in compelling circumstances, necessitating Miranda warnings, and thus the evidence resulting from the interrogation must be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision and the circuit court's judgments, ruling that the interrogation occurred in compelling circumstances and the evidence must be suppressed.

title: State v. Benton
description: Whether a private citizen, Layman, became a state agent for purposes of Article I, section 11, of the Oregon Constitution, and if so, when that agency began.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Layman was never acting as an agent for the state when questioning defendant, and therefore all of Layman's testimony is admissible.
defendant_argument: Defendant argued that Layman had acted as a state agent from the beginning of his interactions with defendant, and therefore none of Layman's testimony is admissible.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that Layman became a state agent after his second proffer meeting on July 2, 2015, and therefore defendant's statements made after that date should have been excluded, reversing and remanding defendant's convictions on Counts 1, 2, 6, and 7 for a new trial.

title: State ex rel Rosenblum v. Living Essentials, LLC
description: Whether the Unlawful Trade Practices Act (UTPA) provisions ORS 646.608(1)(b) and (1)(e) contain an implicit requirement that defendants' acts were "material to consumer purchasing decisions."
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, the State of Oregon, argued that the UTPA provisions do not require proof that misrepresentations were "material to consumer purchasing decisions" and that the lower courts erred in adding this implicit requirement.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the UTPA provisions implicitly require proof of materiality to consumer purchasing decisions and that without such a requirement, the provisions facially violate free speech protections under the state and federal constitutions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, concluding that the UTPA provisions at issue do not contain a "material to consumer purchasing decisions" requirement and are not facially unconstitutional, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Craigen
description: Whether detectives violated the defendant's right to counsel under Article I, section 11, of the Oregon Constitution by questioning him about charged crimes (felon in possession of a firearm) without his counsel present, and whether the evidence obtained from this questioning must be suppressed in his murder trial.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the questioning was primarily about the uncharged murder, for which the right to counsel had not yet attached, and therefore, suppression of evidence was not required.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that detectives explicitly questioned him about the charged FIP crimes, on which he was represented by counsel, violating his Article I, section 11 right to counsel, and thus all resulting evidence must be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, which found that the trial court erred in denying the defendant's motion to suppress, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Colgrove
description: Whether ORS 138.105(5) precludes a defendant who has pleaded guilty or no contest from obtaining appellate review of legal challenges to the conviction in the judgment entered in the trial court.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Oregon (respondent) argued that ORS 138.105(5) precludes appellate review of legal challenges to a conviction based on a guilty or no contest plea, interpreting "conviction" as the judicial determination of guilt reflected in the judgment.
defendant_argument: Rhonda Colgrove (petitioner) argued that ORS 138.105(5) should be read narrowly, interpreting "conviction" as "finding of guilt" to allow appellate review of legal challenges to the entry of a judgment of conviction, such as erroneous termination of diversion, and that precluding such review would be unconstitutional.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, concluding that ORS 138.105(5) precludes appellate review of legal challenges to the conviction in the judgment entered in the trial court. The circuit court's judgment of conviction was affirmed in part and vacated in part, and the case was remanded for further proceedings, with the judgment for costs of appointed counsel reversed.

title: State v. Ralston
description: Whether the defendant's right to a speedy trial under the Oregon Constitution was violated due to delays in prosecution that resulted in the automatic overwriting of booking video evidence, which the defendant claimed prejudiced his defense.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the delays were largely explained and reasonable, and that the defendant failed to demonstrate a reasonable possibility of prejudice from the lost booking video, as its destruction was a happenstance unrelated to any unreasonable delay.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the state's unexplained delays in prosecution led to the automatic overwriting of the booking video, which constituted prejudice to his defense by depriving him of crucial objective evidence, thereby violating his speedy trial right.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, upholding the denial of the defendant's motion to dismiss based on speedy-trial grounds, concluding that the defendant failed to establish a causal connection between the delay and the prejudice from the lost video.

title: State v. Thompson
description: Whether the five-day warrantless retention of a cell phone by police was an unlawful seizure under Article I, section 9, of the Oregon Constitution, and if so, whether evidence derived from it should have been suppressed.
plaintiff_argument: The defendant (Thompson) argued that the police's five-day retention of his cell phone without a warrant was unlawful and that all evidence derived from this unlawful seizure, including his interview statements, should have been suppressed.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the initial seizure and subsequent retention of the phone were lawful due to probable cause and exigent circumstances (fear of evidence destruction and an active investigation), and that any error in admitting derivative evidence was harmless.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the five-day retention of the defendant's phone was unlawful and that some interview statements should have been suppressed, but ultimately affirmed the defendant's conviction because the error was harmless.

title: State v. Gray
description: Whether Article I, section 11, of the Oregon Constitution entitles a defendant to have counsel present in the grand jury room during their testimony, with the defendant arguing it is a critical stage of prosecution requiring counsel, and the state arguing that grand jury proceedings are closed and the statute does not create such a right.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that grand jury proceedings are closed by statute to all but designated persons, not including a witness's attorney, and that the legislature did not intend to create a statutory or constitutional right to counsel's presence in the grand jury room.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his voluntary appearance before the grand jury is a 'critical stage' of the prosecution, triggering his state constitutional right to have counsel present in the grand jury room during his testimony.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that a defendant has a state constitutional right to have counsel present in the grand jury room for consultation during their grand jury testimony, and issued a peremptory writ.

title: State ex rel. Kristof v. Fagan
description: Whether Nicholas Kristof met the three-year residency requirement to be eligible to run for governor in Oregon, with the plaintiff arguing for a looser interpretation of "resident" and the defendant arguing for a strict "domicile" standard.
plaintiff_argument: Nicholas Kristof argued for a looser interpretation of "resident" that would allow him to be considered a resident of Oregon despite connections to New York, and that the durational residency requirement is unconstitutional under strict scrutiny.
defendant_argument: Secretary of State Shemia Fagan argued that "resident" means "domicile," requiring a single, fixed habitation with intent to remain, and that Kristof did not meet this standard, and that the residency requirement is not subject to strict scrutiny.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed Kristof's petition for a writ of mandamus, upholding the Secretary of State's determination that he did not meet the residency requirement.

title: Whitehead v. Fagan
description: Whether the Secretary of State is required to count the signatures on an initiative petition of voters whose registration is deemed "inactive".
plaintiff_argument: Inactive registered voters are still "qualified voters" under Article IV, section 1, and their signatures on initiative petitions should be counted.
defendant_argument: Voters with inactive registration are not "registered in the manner provided by law" and thus not "qualified voters" under Article IV, section 1, so their signatures should not be counted.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Secretary of State was not required to count signatures from voters with inactive registration on initiative petitions, reversing the Court of Appeals decision and affirming the circuit court.

title: State v. McCarthy
description: Whether a warrantless search of a vehicle is justified under the "automobile exception" without actual exigent circumstances, or if actual exigent circumstances must be proven by the state.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the warrantless search of the truck was justified under the "automobile exception," which presumes exigent circumstances if the vehicle was mobile when stopped and there was probable cause, without needing to prove actual exigency.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the warrantless search of the truck violated Article I, section 9, of the Oregon Constitution, and that the "automobile exception's" per se exigency rule should be overruled to require proof of actual exigent circumstances at the time of the search.
decision_outcome: The court overruled the "per se exigency rule" of the automobile exception, holding that the state must prove actual exigent circumstances for a warrantless vehicle search, and affirmed the trial court's decision to suppress the evidence.

title: State v. Keys
description: Whether a defective waiver of a preliminary hearing deprives a circuit court of subject matter jurisdiction, with the plaintiff arguing it is not a jurisdictional defect and the defendant arguing it is.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that a defective waiver of a preliminary hearing is not a jurisdictional defect, but rather a personal constitutional right that must be raised below or fall under a preservation rule exception.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that an invalid waiver of a preliminary hearing is a jurisdictional issue that can be raised for the first time on appeal, relying on prior court decisions and constitutional amendments.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals decision, holding that a defective waiver of a preliminary hearing does not deprive a circuit court of subject matter jurisdiction, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State ex rel. Kotek v. Fagan
description: Whether the Supreme Court has the authority to extend the constitutional deadlines for legislative reapportionment when federal census data is delayed, and whether such an extension is warranted.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs-relators, on behalf of the Oregon Legislative Assembly, argued that due to the federal government's delayed release of 2020 census data, it is impossible to meet the constitutional deadlines for reapportionment, and requested a writ of mandamus to extend these deadlines and enjoin the Secretary of State from making a plan until the Legislative Assembly has an opportunity to do so with the federal data.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the Oregon Secretary of State, argued that the court lacks the authority to extend the constitutional deadlines and that, even if it did, no extension is warranted. She contended that non-census data could be used for an initial reapportionment plan, with subsequent revisions during judicial review.
decision_outcome: The court allowed the relators' petition for a writ of mandamus, establishing revised deadlines for reapportionment, permitting the Legislative Assembly to enact a plan during an emergency session, and revising the residency timeline for candidates.

title: State v. Pittman
description: Whether compelling a criminal defendant to unlock a passcode-protected cell phone violates their right against self-incrimination under Article I, section 12, of the Oregon Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Compelling the defendant to unlock her phone and provide the passcode would violate her right against self-incrimination because it would provide incriminating, testimonial evidence that she owned or had access to the phone and its contents.
defendant_argument: Even if unlocking the phone is testimonial, its aspects are insignificant because the state already knows the facts (e.g., she possessed the phone and likely knew the passcode) and only seeks access to the phone's contents, not to learn new facts from her act.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, finding that the trial court's order compelling the defendant to unlock her cell phone violated her right against self-incrimination under Article I, section 12, of the Oregon Constitution because the state failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that it already knew the information the act would communicate and did not prohibit the use of the compelled act against the defendant.
